facts.claim: RFC 20 (1969) set out ASCII for network interchange: a 7-bit code, so 128 characters, numbered 0 to 127.
The Unicode Consortium’s page for Unicode 18.0, dated 16 September 2026: it adds 13,007 characters, for a total of 172,808.
The same page for Unicode 18.0: 172,808 characters in total.
Unicode’s glossary: code points run from 0 to 10FFFF in base 16, room for 1,114,112 in all.
RFC 3629: UTF-8 writes each character in 1 to 4 bytes (octets), and US-ASCII characters as one byte each, unchanged.
W3Techs, 30 October 2026: of the websites whose way of writing text as bytes they know, 99.1% use UTF-8.
The WHATWG Encoding Standard treats the names “latin1” and “iso-8859-1” as windows-1252, so browsers read Latin-1 text with the Windows-1252 table.
ECMAScript: a string is a sequence of 16-bit code units, so a character past U+FFFF counts as two in its length.
Unicode’s UAX #29 defines grapheme clusters: what a reader takes as one character, such as emoji joined by zero-width joiners.
ECMA-402, the standard for JavaScript’s language-aware text tools, defines Intl.Segmenter, which splits text into graphemes, words or sentences.

Unicode’s UAX #29 (revision 49, for Unicode 18.0): a limit on graphemes is not a limit on data size, since one grapheme has no size limit, so its example form caps both 300 graphemes and 3,000 UTF-8 bytes.
Unicode’s UAX #15: its NFC form joins e and a separate accent mark into the single code point é, so the same text typed two ways comes out the same.
Unicode’s UTS #39 lists confusables: characters from different scripts that look alike, such as Latin a and Cyrillic а.
Radford et al. (2019) built GPT-2’s word pieces (tokens) on UTF-8 bytes, so it can take in any Unicode text.
